newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Sept too early for NZ savings referendum - ISI.
newsitem.headline: Sept too early for NZ savings referendum - ISI.

text.p: There may be insufficient time to design a viable compulsory retirement savings scheme, educate New Zealand voters on its implications and then hold a referendum by September, the Investment Savings and Insurance Association (ISI) said on Wednesday.
It is vital the government get the process right in reviewing the options for retirement savings, said ISI chief executive Roger Gill, speaking at the ISI's official launch at parliament.
Earlier on Wednesday, Finance Minister Bill Birch said a referendum on compulsory savings would be held no later than September.

If the scheme received public support it would be introduced by July 1, 1998, Birch said, confirming an undertaking in the December 1996 coalition agreement between the National and New Zealand First parties.

Gill said that in determining the future direction of savings policy, the government should also consider the second review by the Todd Taskforce, due later this year, which will assess the present voluntary savings regime.

"If the referendum is held before the Todd review has been completed, there is a danger of getting the cart before the horse. Voters would be asked to make a decision vitally affecting their future security before they had all the facts before them," he said.
Gill said if the previous referendum on the electoral system could be used as a precedent, it suggested the time frame the government had allowed itself for a savings referendum was overly ambitious.
"This is a matter too important to be rushed," he said.

The ISI was also concerned about tax distortions creating problems in the curent savings and investment environment. If tax rules were not reviewed before the proposed referendum, a vote in favour of compulsory superannuation could well force New Zealanders into savings products which incurred unfair tax burdens, Gill said.

He said there was a gap between the marginal tax rate applied to life insurance and superannuation funds, and the tax rate applied to many contributors to these funds. The reductions in the lower marginal tax rates in 1996 had increased the disadvantage for many savers.
The ISI also maintains there is a real problem in clearly defining the boundary between revenue and capital.
"At a time when we are being urged to make our own provision for retirement, it is quite illogical that we have a tax system unfairly penalising collective investment and saving," Gill said.

The ISI, which superseded the Life Office Association and the Investment Funds Association, has 30 members collectively managing more than NZ$20 billion in New Zealanders' savings and investments. --Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 4734746
